sections.h2: What is the Sugar Land city property tax rate?
sections.html:
The City of Sugar Land says its adopted rate for Tax Year 2026 is $0.371116 per $100 of taxable value, adopted after a public hearing on September 8, 2026. That figure covers only the city share of a Sugar Land bill; the school district, Fort Bend County and any MUD or LID levy sit on top of it.

The city splits its rate into two parts: $0.220157 for maintenance and operations and $0.150959 for debt service. Debt service is the portion that repays borrowed money for city projects.

On its own page the city also notes that it makes up about 21 percent of the residential bill in Fort Bend ISD and 19 percent in Lamar CISD, before any MUD or LID taxes. Which district serves your house is printed on your tax bill.

sections.h2: How have Sugar Land's rates changed over three years?
sections.html:
The rate edged up in both Tax Year 2025 and Tax Year 2026. The city publishes a three-year comparison, reproduced below as printed on its site.

City of Sugar Land tax rate per $100, as printed on sugarlandtx.gov

Maintenance and operations$0.220157$0.207172$0.207172
Debt service$0.150959$0.151655$0.146038
Total$0.371116$0.358827$0.353210

The city also lists a no-new-revenue rate of $0.355381 and a voter-approval rate of $0.381586 for 2026. The voter-approval rate is the ceiling the city cannot pass without a vote. For the median homestead the city prints an estimated annual city bill of $1,371 for 2026, against $1,312 the prior year.

sections.h2: How does Sugar Land set its rate each year?
sections.html:
Council adopts the rate in September, after budget approval and a public hearing. The city has 60 days after it receives the certified tax roll, or until September 30, whichever is later, to adopt it. For 2025 the council adopted $0.358827 on September 16, 2025, by Ordinance No. 2387, and for 2026 the hearing was held September 8, 2026.

Two reference rates frame the vote. The no-new-revenue rate raises the same money as the year before from existing property, and the voter-approval rate is the most the city can set without an election. The city describes the voter-approval rate as the revenue needed for debt service plus a 3.5 percent increase in maintenance and operations revenue.

The city also publishes a taxpayer impact statement, stating a $4.90 monthly impact for the median homestead in 2026, and budgeted property tax revenue of $81,205,666 for FY2027. Appraised values are certified by July 25, so the rate cannot be final until that roll is in.

sections.h2: Which exemptions does Sugar Land offer?
sections.html:
The city lists a homestead exemption of 15 percent of assessed value, plus $70,000 for owners who are over 65 and $70,000 for disabled persons. A homeowner who is both over 65 and disabled may receive only one of those two. For disabled veterans, the city tells owners to contact the Fort Bend Central Appraisal District.

These are the city's exemptions. School districts have their own, and the Texas Comptroller prints the state-required school homestead exemption as $140,000, with another $60,000 for seniors and disabled owners. Owners 65 or older or disabled also get a school tax ceiling that generally holds the school bill at the level of the year they first qualified.

  • You must own the home and live in it as your main residence, and claim no other homestead.
  • A buyer who takes title after January 1 may claim the exemption for the rest of that year if the prior owner had not.
  • Applications go to the appraisal district, not to the city.

sections.h2: Who sets the value and who collects the tax in Sugar Land?
sections.html:
The Fort Bend Central Appraisal District sets values, and the Fort Bend County Tax Assessor-Collector bills and collects the money. The city says it contracts with the county assessor-collector for billing and collection, and it sends exemption and valuation questions to the appraisal district.

The appraisal district's office is at 2801 B F Terry Blvd, Rosenberg, TX 77471, and its phone is 281-344-8623, as printed on the Fort Bend County exemption page. That page also says exemption applications need a copy of the applicant's Texas driver's license or DPS ID, and the address on it must match the property address.

Texas appraises property as of January 1. Under the state calendar, notices for single-family homesteads go out around April 1, the usual protest deadline is May 15 or 30 days after notice, and the appraisal records are approved in July. If you disagree with a value, that window is the time to act.

sections.h2: What is the payment deadline in Sugar Land?
sections.html:
Bills are mailed about October 1, payment is due on receipt, and taxes not paid by January 31 become delinquent on February 1. The Comptroller prints that rule for the whole state, so it applies to a Sugar Land house the same way.

Two practical notes from the state pages. A bill mailed late, after January 10, pushes the delinquency date to the first day of the next month that gives at least 21 days. And seniors and disabled owners may split the bill into four installments, with the first due by February 1.

The penalty schedule is steep once a bill goes delinquent.

  • February 1: six percent penalty and one percent interest added.
  • Each month after: penalty grows by one percent until July 1, when it reaches 12 percent.
  • Interest keeps running at one percent a month with no maximum, and an attorney's penalty of up to 20 percent can be added.

sections.h2: Does the tax bill follow a Sugar Land house to a new owner?
sections.html:
The lien for each year's tax attaches January 1, and it stays with the property when ownership changes. A buyer cannot get clear title until delinquent taxes are paid, and the owner on January 1 can still be sued for the tax after a sale.

That is why a title company asks for a tax certificate and settles anything owed from your proceeds. If you are behind, the collection path runs from delinquent notices to an installment plan to a lawsuit, with court costs added to the bill. A taxing unit can eventually foreclose on the lien and sell the house at auction.

If you are selling because you owe taxes, get a payoff number from the Fort Bend County Tax Assessor-Collector before pricing. Knowing the number lets you compare a listing, a private sale and a cash offer on equal terms. Waiver of penalty and interest is possible in some cases when the tax is paid promptly after you learn of the delinquency, so ask the tax office about that too.

faqs.q: What is the Sugar Land city tax rate for 2026?
faqs.a: It is $0.371116 per $100 of taxable value, according to the City of Sugar Land's adopted-rate page. Your total bill adds school, county and any MUD or LID rates.

faqs.q: Does Sugar Land have a homestead exemption?
faqs.a: Yes. The city lists 15 percent of assessed value for homesteads, $70,000 for over-65 owners and $70,000 for disabled persons, with only one of the last two allowed. Apply through the Fort Bend Central Appraisal District.

faqs.q: Who do I pay my Sugar Land property tax to?
faqs.a: The Fort Bend County Tax Assessor-Collector, which bills and collects for the city under a contract. Questions about value or exemptions go to the Fort Bend Central Appraisal District.

faqs.q: When does a Sugar Land bill turn delinquent?
faqs.a: January 31 for most owners. Unpaid taxes become delinquent February 1 and draw a six percent penalty plus one percent interest that day.

faqs.q: Can I sell my Sugar Land house if I owe back taxes?
faqs.a: Yes. The title company pays the delinquent tax and penalties from your sale proceeds at closing, so get a payoff amount from the county tax office first.
